14.4 Exercise #3
The Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS) project provides consistent multiband surface reflectance (SR) data from NASA/USGS Landsat 8 and Landsat 9 satellites (using Operational Land Imager, OLI) and Europe’s Copernicus Sentinel-2A and Sentinel-2B satellites (using Multi-Spectral Instrument, MSI). These measurements provide global land observations with a 2–3 days temporal frequency at 30-meter spatial resolution. Sample rasters for band 4 (Red) and band 5 (Near-Infrared) from this resource are provided at the following location in the sample data: “./SampleData-master/raster_files/landsat/”
For LANDSAT 8, the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (a proxy for vegetation health) is calculated as:
\[
NDVI=(Band 5- Band 4)/(Band 5+ Band 4)
\] For more information on the HSL products, bands and applications, please refer to: https://lpdaac.usgs.gov/data/get-started-data/collection-overview/missions/harmonized-landsat-sentinel-2-hls-overview/

Imagine that a federal agency is interested in understanding the impacts of land conservation practices to improve carbon sequestration in the soil. The agency has selected two potential Carbon Sequestration Testbed (CST) sites across Louisiana. Using the observations of hydrometeorological, land practice, and vegetation datasets collected from these locations, the agency is interested in developing a physics-based ecohydrology model to mimic the interactions between soil, plants, and atmosphere at these test beds. This will help develop predictive models to estimate the effects of various management practices on the carbon sequestration potential in soil.

library(terra)

# Import vector for Louisiana

14.6 Exercise #5
Soil moisture is an important hydrological variable with strong linkages to crop health and yield. Satellites such as NASA’s SMAP and ESA’s SMOS provide soil moisture information for the surface profile (0-5 cm). However, temporal variability in the surface soil moisture gets attenuated and dampened as water infiltrates through the soil layers. This is followed by evapotranspirative losses to the atmosphere from the rootzone. The time delay in surface soil moisture and evapotranspiration variability indicates several critical aspects of ecosystem functioning, terrestrial water and energy balance and soil hydraulic processes.
In this exercise, we will simulate the attenuation and dampening effect on the surface soil moisture using a moving average filter and study how increasing smoothing of surface soil moisture correlates with the variability in evapotranspiration. We will use simulated gridded surface soil moisture and evapotranspiration from VIC land surface model for the year 2011.


Download CONUS-wide daily simulated soil moisture (soilmoist.2011.nc) and evapotranspiration (et.2011.nc) for the year 2011 from NOAA-PSL’s servers. using the following file location:
sm_path = "https://downloads.psl.noaa.gov//Datasets/livneh/fluxvars/soilmoist.2011.nc"
et_path = "https://downloads.psl.noaa.gov//Datasets/livneh/fluxvars/et.2011.nc"



Import the downloaded netCDFs to workspace as spatRasters. Print the time stamp and variable names of the two spatRasters using terra::time() and terra::names() functions. You will notice that et.2011.nc has one raster layer for each day. soilmoist.2011.nc contains three raster layers (one for each soil profile level) per day.



Create a new multilayer spatRaster for raster layers for soil profile level 1. (Hint: using substr() on the layer names() from soilmoist.2011.nc, subset the layers with lev= “1” in their name)



Create a polygon with with extent: xmin=255, xmax=265, ymin=40, ymax=48.

title: 12  Surface-Rootzone Soil Hydrologic Connectivity
text:
12.1 Surface-Rootzone Soil Hydrologic Connectivity
While soil moisture’s centrality in precipitation partitioning into groundwater recharge and surface runoff is widely recognized, often the criticality of the surface and rootzone connectivity is overlooked. You might have read about incessant rainfall after a dry and hot period often generates flash floods. Why? Because the surface profile might get hydrophobic, and hence, hydrologically decoupled from the rootzone under intense heat. So, a larger fraction of the incoming rain contributes to overland runoff instead of infiltrating to the rootzone, and contributing to the groundwater recharge. So, hydrologic connectivity between surface and the rootzone profile directly affects critical ecohydrological processes such as groundwater recharge, surface runoff generation, and the overall water availability for ecosystem sustenance. Needless to say, knowing how moisture moves from the surface to the rootzone can improved water management to ensure sustained and adequate moisture to the crops, while preventing over-irrigation. Accurate data on both surface and rootzone soil moisture also helps in improving weather forecasts and seasonal-scale climate forecasts, thereby helping to predict and manage hydrologic extremes such as droughts and floods.
In this chapter, we will explore the hydrologic relationship between surface and the rootzone profile, and methods to simulate these processes.

We can notice that the temporal response of surface soil moisture to a precipitation varies significantly compared to that of the deeper profile. Surface soil moisture reacts almost immediately to precipitation. This layer, typically the top few centimeters, quickly absorbs rainfall, leading to a rapid increase in moisture content. Similarly, the surface, having exposed to atmospheric conditions, also dries out rapidly due to evaporation and plant water uptake. In contrast, soil moisture from the rootzone (typically up to about 1 meter) responds more slowly to precipitation as it relies on the infiltration of water from the surface layer. As infiltration delays moisture transfer to the rootzone profile. This results in a delayed but more gradual increase in rootzone moisture content. Similarly, rootzone also retains water longer. This ensures a more consistent and reliable source of water for plant growth and ecosystem stability. A similar behavior can also be seen in the temperature distribution within the soil profile. The difference in the temporal response of rootzone moisture and thermal fluxes vis-à-vis surface profile is essentially a natural manifestation of a low pass filter, where the high-frequency variations (rapid changes) in surface soil moisture or temperature are filtered out, leaving only the low-frequency variations (slower, more sustained changes) to affect the rootzone.

12.2 Simulating Low-pass Filtering of Meteorological Perturbations Through Soil Profile
Under hydrologic equilibrium, the analytical solution of the 1-dimensional vertical water balance (differential) equation can be approximated using the relationship between the temporal changes in the rootzone soil moisture (RZSM) and the difference in SSM vis-à-vis the antecedent rootzone conditions (Wagner et al., 1999, Albergel et al., 2008, Manfreda et al., 2014). A simple recursive exponential low-pass filter to simulate the 1-dimensional first-order infinite-impulse response of RZSM to temporal variability in SSM is given as follows:
\[ RZSM_t^{'}= RZSM_{t-1}^{'}+ D_p(SSM_t-RZSM_{t-1}^{'})  \tag{12.1}\]
where, \(t \ge1\); when \(t=1\), \(RZSM_{t=0}^{'}=SSM_{t=0}\).
\(RZSM_{t}^{'}\) is the temporally smoothed (filtered) SSM at time \(t\) .
Parameter \(D_p\) is the exponential filter smoothing factor of the soil profile \([-]\), also called the pseudo-diffusivity coefficient; \(D_p\) ∈ [0,1]. It represents the effective influence of various bio-geo-physical controls such as vegetation, topography, hydroclimatology and pedological characteristics (soil profile thickness, effective soil hydraulic characteristics, etc.) on vertical fluxes between the soil surface and the rootzone.
Eq. 1 provides a first-order approximation of the infinite-impulse response of RZSM to temporal variability in SSM as \(RZSM^{'}\), and yields the exponential weighted average of the antecedent observations using weights proportional to the terms of the geometric progression: \(1, (1-D_p), (1-D_p)^2, ….(1-D_p)^n\), \(-\) the discrete form of an exponential function (Hunter, 1986; Perry, 2010). This method makes two key assumption:

The lateral moisture flux to/from the rootzone is negligible, and,
The groundwater table is significantly deeper than the rootzone depth.


12.2.1 Origins of Low-pass Filter Relationship in Vertical Soil Fluxes
The origins of the low-pass filter effect of soil profile on surface variability in soil moisture can be traced to the original equations for vertical flux of water int he unsaturated soil profile. We recall the Diffusivity version of Richard’s equation as follows:
\[
\frac{\partial\theta} {\partial t}= \frac{\partial}{\partial z}(D(\theta)\frac{\partial\theta}{\partial z})-\frac{\partial K(\theta)}{\partial z}
\tag{12.2}\]
where, \(D\) and \(K\) are the hydraulic diffusivity and conductivity of the soil profile, and are a function of the water content of the soil profile, \(z\) is the height above the bottom of the soil profile and \(\theta\) is the soil moisture content. The right hand side of this equation contains two terms, where \(\partial/\partial z (D(\theta)\partial/\partial z)\) accounts for the flux due to the suction gradient in the profile, while \(\partial K(\theta)/\partial z\) pertains to the role of gravity in the vertical flow of water. Given the equivalent suction exerted by the atmosphere is several order of magnitude compare to the gravitational head gradient, we can simplify the preceeding equation as:
\[
\frac{\partial\theta} {\partial t}= \frac{\partial}{\partial z}(D(\theta)\frac{\partial\theta}{\partial z})
\tag{12.3}\]
First integral of this equation can be written as: \[
\frac{d\theta}{dt}=D(\theta)\frac{d\theta}{dz}+C
\tag{12.4}\] where, \(C\) is the constant of integration. Since there is no flow at the bottom boundary of the soil profile, \(d\theta/dz=0\) . Hence, \(C=0\). Writing the preceding equation in discrete form, we get:
\[
\frac{\Delta\theta}{\Delta t}=D(\theta)\frac{\Delta\theta}{\Delta z}
\tag{12.5}\]
As the soil reaches the second phase of drying, it enters a phase where the rate of soil drydown is slow, and the rate of loss of water from all depths can be assumed to be the same. Simplifying the previous equation for a simple 2-layer representation of soil profile, with \(SSM\) and \(RZSM\) representing the surface and rootzone soil moisture respectively, we can write Eq. 5 as: \[
RZSM_t-RZSM_{t-1}= D(RZSM) \times (SSM_{t}-RZSM_{t-1})
\] or, \[
RZSM_t=RZSM_{t-1}+ D(RZSM) \times (SSM_{t}-RZSM_{t-1})
\tag{12.6}\]
However, such coarse discretization of the soil profile may not account for the different initial values of true surface and rootzone soil moisture, and may lead to a systematic bias in the estimated values of \(RZSM\) using the low-pass filter approach compared to the observations. This equation becomes analogous to the exponential infinite impulse response low-pass filter equation provided in Eq. 1 earlier. The filtered surface soil moisture i.e. \(RZSM'\) can be related to the true rootzone SM through a linear transformation as: \(RZSM= C \times RZSM^{'}+\epsilon\), where, \(C\) is the ratio of the dynamic range of \(RZSM\) and \(RZSM'\) as follows: \[
C= \frac {\max(RZSM)-min(RZSM)} {max(RZSM^{'})-min(RZSM^{'})}
\tag{12.7}\] and, \[
\epsilon=min(RZSM)-C \times min(RZSM^{'})
\tag{12.8}\]






Note



Hydraulic diffusivity (or pseudo-diffusivity) is a function of the hydrologic state of the rootzone. However, since the true form of the relationship between \(D-RZSM\) or \(Dp-RZSM^{'}\) is not known in the field, the value of \(D\) and \(D_p\) is often assumed to be constant for simplicity.




12.2.2 Propagation of Drying Front in the Soil Profile
We will demonstrate the application of the low-pass filter discussed above to capture the propagation of drying front from the surface to the deeper profiles at the test site.The function lp_filt takes the SSM as input, apply a low-pass infinite impulse response filter on the time series for the user-specified \(Dp\), and returns the filtered SSM (SSMf). In contrast, the wetting front propagation is represented as a pulse which is passed down to the filtered soil moisture in the preceding time step.This assumption is reasonably valid at the daily time scale at which this example is applied.

# Function for implementing LP filter on surface soil moisture
lp_filt=function(SSM, Dp){
  # PARAMETERS---
  #   SSM= Surface soil moisture
  #   Dp= Pseudo-diffusivity coefficient
  SSMf=c()                           # Empty array to store filtered SSM 
  buffer=0.01*(max(SSM)-min(SSM))    # To decrease sensitivity to noise in sensor readings (1% of SSM range)

  # Apply recursive filter
  SSMf[1]=SSM[1]                    # Initialize the series
  for (t in 2:length(SSM)) 
  SSMf[t]=ifelse(SSM[t] > (SSM[t-1]+buffer),max(SSM[t], SSMf[t-1]),SSMf[t-1]+Dp*(SSM[t]-SSMf[t-1]))
  return(SSMf) 
}

# Filtered surface soil moisture with varying values of Dp
SSM=SMpdf$SM5   # Surface soil moisture
SSMf_1=lp_filt(SSM, Dp= 0.1)
SSMf_05=lp_filt(SSM, Dp= 0.05)
SSMf_02=lp_filt(SSM, Dp= 0.02)

# Plot surface soil moisture with filtered time series
plot(SSM, type="l", col="gray80", lwd=3, ylab="Value", xlab="Time", 
main="Filtered v/s observed SSM for varying Dp")
lines(SSMf_1, col="red")
lines(SSMf_05, col="purple")
lines(SSMf_02, col="blue")
legend(x = "bottomleft",        
       legend = c("SSM","Dp=0.1", "Dp=0.05", "Dp=0.02"),  
       lty = c(1,1,1,1),           
       col = c("gray80","red","purple","blue"),           
       lwd = 1, bty = "n")        














Note



We observe that the low-pass filter is only applied during the drydown phase of the surface soil moisture moisture. As the value of \(D_p\) decreases, the rate of drydown in \(SM^{'}\) decreases due to the increase in the e-folding time of the exponential filter applied.


Multi-depth soil moisture records are used to calculate the effective soil moisture for the 0-100 cm profile, which serves as the observed rootzone soil moisture for our purpose. We will take a weighted average of the multi-depth observations based on the profile represented by each observation depth. We will now use Eq 8-9 to estimate the rootzone soil moisture from surface observations. But first, we will select the value of \(D_{p}\) which yield a filtered surface soil moisture with highest correlation with the observed rootzone soil moisture. Once we determine the optimum value of \(D_{p}\) (either by optimization, or by trial and error), we will use it to filter SSM. This time series will be assumed to be representative of the temporal dynamics of the rootzone soil moisture.

# Weighted average of soil moisture at multiple depths to estimate RZSM
RZSM=(SMpdf$SM5*(7.5-0)+          # 0- 7.5 cm depth
      SMpdf$SM10*(15-7.5)+        # 7.5-15 cm depth
      SMpdf$SM20*(35-15)+         # 15-35 cm depth
      SMpdf$SM50*(75-35)+         # 35-75 cm depth
      SMpdf$SM100*(100-75))/100   # 75-100 cm depth

# Note Dp=0.1 yields maximum correlation with RZSM
c(cor(RZSM, SSMf_02), cor(RZSM, SSMf_05),cor(RZSM, SSMf_1))

[1] 0.8317762 0.9283331 0.9322160

# Transform the filtered SM to RZSM using the linear transformation parameters 
C=(max(RZSM)-min(RZSM))/(max(SSMf_1)-min(SSMf_1))
epsilon=min(RZSM)-C*min(SSMf_1)
RZSM_est=C*SSMf_1+epsilon

# Plotting estimated versus observed RZSM
plot(RZSM, type="l", col="gray80", lwd=3, ylab="Volumetric SM", xlab="Time", 
main="Comparison of obs. vs est. RZSM", ylim=c(0,0.5))
lines(SSM, col="red")
lines(RZSM_est, col="blue")
legend(x = "bottomleft",        
       legend = c("RZSM", "SSM", "est. RZSM"),  
       lty = c(1,1,1),           
       col = c("gray80","red","blue"),           
       lwd = 1, bty = "n")   








Conversely, the low-pass filter can be inverted to estimate the surface soil moisture using the rootzone soil moisture in an iterative form. Use of this equation can be very helpful in a scenario where surface soil moisture observations are available (for example, from remote-sensing observations) and a simplistic representation of soil water balance for the profile can simultaneously generate equivalent surface soil moisture estimates for model training and validation.

# Inverting low pass filter for SSM estimation from filtered time series
Dp=0.1
buffer=0.01*(max(SSM)-min(SSM))  # To decrease sensitivity to noise in sensor readings (1% of SSM range)
invLP_filt=function(RZSM){
  SSMest=c()
  SSMest[1]=RZSM[1]
  for (t in 2:length(RZSM)){
  SSMest[t]=ifelse(RZSM[t]>(RZSM[t-1]+buffer),
                   min(RZSM[t],SSMf_1[t-1]),
                   (SSMf_1[t-1]+((SSMf_1[t]-SSMf_1[t-1])/Dp)))
  }
return(SSMest)
}

# Apply LP filter inversion
SSMest=invLP_filt(RZSM)

# Plot observed v/s estimated Surface soil moisture
{plot(SSM, type="l", col="gray80", lwd=3, ylab="Volumetric SM", xlab="Time", 
main="Comparison of obs. vs est. SSM", ylim=c(0,0.55))
lines(SSMest, col="red")
lines(RZSM, col="blue")
legend(x = "bottomleft",        
       legend = c("SSM", "est. SSM", "RZSM"),  
       lty = c(1,1,1),           
       col = c("gray80","red","blue"),           
       lwd = 1, bty = "n") }








Estimating rootzone soil moisture using a low-pass filter and surface soil moisture is efficient but challenging due to the lack of spatially contiguous rootzone soil moisture records for filter calibration. Observations of rootzone soil moisture are only available through a sparse network of observation stations. Some studies use land-surface model simulations for this purpose, but these can only replicate the pre-defined functional relationships in the models and are affected by significant disagreements between models due to different treatments of subgrid-scale heterogeneity in soil and vegetation properties. Additionally, the “active” rootzone layer, which is crucial for root-water uptake and land-atmosphere interactions, varies significantly across different regions. This variability is influenced by factors such as climate (temperature, radiation, and precipitation patterns), vegetation (rooting patterns and water uptake depth), and landscape characteristics (albedo and soil type). In contrast, most land-surface models assume a fixed rootzone depth, typically between 1 and 2 meters.

14.1 Model Description
Landscape-scale Soil Hydrology Model is a 2-layer soil water balance model which works based on the emergent signature of terrestrial water-energy coupling beyond the pedon scale scale. As general schematic of the model with key model variables is given below:






14.1.1 Background
The nature of the soil-vegetation-atmosphere (SVA) interactions evolve with changes in the rootzone soil moisture. This transition of soil hydrologic state from energy-limited to water-limited regimes is represented as a sigmoid curve, with three distinct phases. Abundance of soil moisture in the SVA system can be characterized as wet decoupled, characterized by weakened linkages between water–carbon–energy cycles due to limiting net radiation and atmospheric resistance, with ET losses close to (or at) the potential rate. As the soil begins to dry, soil moisture has higher control over the temporal variability of ET and is characterized by strong land-atmospheric coupling. As soil dries further, soil moisture can not sustain high atmospheric moisture demand, and evapotranspiration again decouples from the rootzone soil moisture.
The connections between soil water balance, noise-induced variability in climatic forces, and positive land-atmospheric feedback lead to dynamic transitions in soil moisture, potentially resulting in a preferred hydrologic states. When one or more state variables are disturbed, or stress (such as atmospheric moisture demand causing evapotranspirative losses) is gradually increased, the SVA system may shift into a new hydrologic regime. Sustained dry-average conditions reinforce dry anomalies (low evaporation results in low regional precipitation and dry soils, leading to even lower evaporation). Conversely, precipitation can alter the soil hydrologic state to wet-average conditions, thereby increasing regional evaporation and precipitation through moisture recycling. If \(\theta_{r}\) represents rootzone soil moisture, then the threshold at which hydrologic tipping of rootzone soil moisture from wet-to-dry-preferential state occurs is represented at \(\theta_{X, r}\), which is called the “tipping” point of the rootzone soil hydrological regimes (Sehgal and Mohanty 2024).





This relationship between rootzone soil moisture and evaporative fraction (evapotranspiration over potential evapotranspiration) is represented as a sigmoid function given below:
\[
EF=\frac{ET}{PET}=\frac{EF_{r,mx}}{\left(1+\left|\left(\frac{\theta_{X, r}\left(\theta_r-1\right)}{\left(1-\theta_{X, r}\right) \theta_r}\right)\right|^m\right)}
\]
Here, \(EF_{r,mx}\) represents the maximum evaporative fraction sustainable by the SVA system. The tipping point of soil moisture is represented as \(\theta_{X}\). Land-atmospheric coupling strength is represented by the parameter \(m\). The input vertical flux to the soil below the surface is considered to be derived from the drainage of the surface profile, which is a non-linear function of the field capacity \(\theta_{fc}\), saturated hydraulic conductivity (\(K_{s}\)), porosity (\(\eta\)) and an empirical power coefficient, \(b\). The same equation is adopted for the rootzone to estimate deep drainage.
\[
D=K_S\left(\frac{\left(\max \left(0, \theta-\theta_{f c}\right)\right)}{\eta-\theta_{f c}}\right)^b
\]
Surface runoff is estimated as the saturation excess component of the precipitation, based on the hydrologic state of the surface profile. Surface evaporation is considered as a fraction \(Es_{frac}\) of the net evapotranspiration. The depth of the surface and the rootzone profile are fixed and are assumed to be 0-5 and 0-100 cm respectively.


14.1.2 Priestley-Taylor Method for Potential ET (PET)
The model uses Priestley-Taylor equation for potential ET estimation. This formulation is based on physical principles and can be seen as a simplified version of the Penman-Monteith formula for calculating evapotranspiration. The simplification involves removing the aerodynamic terms from the Penman-Monteith equation and using a constant (\(α\)), which has been empirically derived and is estimated to be 1.26 for open bodies of water, but can range from <1 (humid conditions) to almost 2 (arid conditions). This constant tends to be higher in arid regions or areas experiencing significant water stress. The Priestley-Taylor formula can be used for calculating daily evapotranspiration and can also be applied to smaller time intervals (hourly, for example) if the necessary data is available.
\[ \text { PET }=\left(\frac{\alpha}{\lambda_v \rho_{\mathrm{w}}}\right) \times \frac{\Delta}{\Delta+\gamma} \times \text {R}  \]
if \(T_{mean}< 0^oC\)
\[ \Delta=0.3405 \times \mathrm{e}^\left(0.0642 \mathrm{~T}_{\text {mean}}\right) \\ \]
if \(T_{mean}> 0^oC\) \[ \Delta=0.3221 \times \mathrm{e}^\left(0.0803 \mathrm{~T}_{\mathrm{mean}}^{0.8876}\right) \]
where,

\(PET\)= Daily potential evapotranspiration (\(m\))
\(λv\) = Latent heat of vaporization (2260 \(kJ/kg\))
\(ρw\) = Density of water (1000 \(kg/m^3\))
\(γ\) = Psychrometric constant ( 4.95x \(10^{-4}\) \(kg/m^3/^oC\))
\(Rad\) = Daily solar radiation incident on a horizontal earth surface (\(kg/m^2\))
\(Δ\) = Slope of the saturation vapor density curve from the psychrometric chart (\(kg/^oC\))
\(T_{mean}\) = Daily mean air temperature (\(^oC\))
\(\alpha\) = Priestley-Taylor correction factor

For use with this model, we will use global, high resolution (30arc-sec) estimates of PT correction factor from (Aschonitis et al. 2017). The dataset will be masked to the extent of the region-of-interest at the time of model implementation. Let’s view the values of Priestley-Taylor correction factor for Contiguous US.

utils::download.file("https://github.com/Vinit-Sehgal/SampleData/blob/master/raster_files/priestley_taylor_coefficient/cropPTalpha.tif?raw=true",
                     destfile = "cropPTalpha.tif", 
                     mode="wb", #wb is write binary
                     method ='auto', 
                     quiet=FALSE)
PTalpha=rast("cropPTalpha.tif")

14.2 Catchment Hydrology with LaSH model

14.2.1 MOPEX Catchments
MOPEX (Model Parameter Estimation Experiment, (Schaake, Cong, and Duan 2006)) catchments are a collection of hydrological catchments across the continental United States used for studying and modeling various aspects of hydrology. These catchments are part of a large dataset that includes daily measurements of evaporation, precipitation, streamflow, and temperature, along with other properties such as drainage area, elevation, and slope. The primary goal of the MOPEX initiative is to improve the understanding and prediction of hydrological processes by providing a comprehensive dataset for model calibration and validation. We will use one of the MOPEX catchments in Louisiana for the demonstration of LaSH model at catchment scale (Duan et al. 2006).

library(terra)   # for spatial data manipulation
library(mapview) # for spatial data visualization

MOPEX=vect("./SampleData-master/MOPEX/MOPEX_catchments_431.shp")

# Display the MOPEX catchments
mapview(MOPEX, col.regions="blue", lwd=2, legend=TRUE, layer.name="MOPEX Catchments")  




# List of LA catchments: 107, 427, 141, 406, 185
mymopex=MOPEX[427,1]
plot(mymopex, col="gray88", lwd=2, main="Selected catchment in Louisiana")







# Extract the extent of the catchment. We will download Met data matching this extent
mopex_ext=ext(mymopex) 



14.2.2 Meteorological Variables
One might recollect Daymet dataset from Chapter 6. We will use Daymet dataset, version 4 (Thornton et al. 1850) as a source of high-resolution, daily surface weather data for the sample catchment. This dataset offers gridded estimates of various weather parameters such as: Minimum and maximum temperature, Precipitation, Shortwave radiation, Vapor pressure, Snow water equivalent and Day length. Appropriate transformation is applied to the dataset to transform the variables to the necessary units.

14.4 Model Application for the catchment
Using the dataset and model parameters, we will apply the LaSH model to each grid to generate spatially distributed outputs of hydrological variables.

############################################################################################
# Soil Water Balance Model
############################################################################################
# Soil moisture values for model initiation
ini_cond=rast(pcpcrp[[1]]) # Generate empty raster to store values using PCP raster as sample
values(ini_cond)=0.25      # Initial soil moisture condition
names(ini_cond)="ini_condition"

# Create a raster stack with all input parameters
ParInRas=c(parDist, ini_cond, alpha) 
# Create a raster stack with all forcing variables
forcingRas=c(pcpcrp, (tmaxcrp+tmincrp)/2, sradcrp) 
SWB_model=function(ParIn,forcing){
  
  # Input parameters  
  SMrx=ParIn[1]         # Rootzone crossing point 
  mr=ParIn[2]           # LA coupling strength  
  EFrmx=ParIn[3]        # Max rootzone Evaporative fraction 
  Es_frac=ParIn[4]      # Surface evaporation fraction: E/Total ET
  
  por_s=ParIn[5]        # Surface porosity
  por_r=ParIn[6]        # Rootzone porosity
  b_s=ParIn[7]          # Power coefficient of surface drainage curve
  b_r=ParIn[8]          # Power coefficient of rootzone drainage curve
  Ks_s=ParIn[9]         # Surface Saturated hydraulic conductivity 
  Ks_r=ParIn[10]        # Rootzone Saturated hydraulic conductivity 
  fc_s=ParIn[11]        # Surface field capacity
  
  ini_condition=ParIn[12]        # Initial SM condition 
  alphaVal= ParIn[13]            # Priestley-Taylor coefficient
  
  spinup=20             # Excluded from the model evaluation
  zs=5                  # Surface layer depth (cm)
  zr=95                 # Difference between rootzone and surface profile depth (cm)
  
  # Rootzone SWRP
  fc_r=SMrx+EFrmx/(2*mr)
  wp_r=pmax(0.02,(SMrx-EFrmx/(2*mr)))
  
  # Forcings
  PCP=forcing[1:(length(forcing)/3)]
  Tmean=forcing[(1+(length(forcing)/3)): (2*(length(forcing)/3))]
  Rad=forcing[(2*(length(forcing)/3)+1):length(forcing)]
  
  PT_PET<<-function(Tmean,Rad,alpha){
    lambdaV= 2260                  # Latent heat of vaporization 
    rhoW= 1000                     # Density of water 
    gamma= 4.95*1e-4               # Psychrometric constant
    
    deltaVal=rep(0, length(Tmean))  # Create empty array
    
    # When Tmean<0
    deltaVal[Tmean<0]=0.3405*exp(0.0642*Tmean[Tmean<0])
    # When Tmean>=0
    deltaVal[Tmean>=0]=0.3221*exp(0.0803*((Tmean[Tmean>=0])^0.8876))
    
    # Priestley-Taylor equation 
    PETval=(alpha/(lambdaV*rhoW))*(deltaVal/(deltaVal+gamma))*Rad
    PETval[PETval<0]=0
    return(PETval) #estimate in m
  }
  
  #~~~ Simple Soil Water Balance Model 
  # Empty arrays to store data
  RZSM= SSM= drainage= ETr= ETs=PET= runoff= infilt =infilCap=c()  
  SSM[1]= RZSM[1]= ini_condition            # Initial soil moisture state
  for (t in 2:length(PCP)){
    
    infilCap[t]= pmax(0,(por_s-SSM[t-1])*zs)
    runoff[t]=pmax(0,(PCP[t]-infilCap[t]))
    
    infilt[t]= Ks_s*(pmax(0,SSM[t-1]-fc_s)/(por_s-fc_s))^b_s
    SSM[t]=pmin(por_s,(pmax(0.02,
                            (zs*SSM[t-1]+pmin(PCP[t],infilCap[t])-infilt[t])/zs)))
    
    # 4. Calculate surface evaporation for days with no PCP 
    PET[t]=100*PT_PET(Tmean[t],Rad[t],alpha=alphaVal)  #PET in cm
    
    # Estimate ET based on PET and RZSM state
    ETr[t]=PET[t]*EFrmx/(1+(abs((SMrx*(RZSM[t-1]-1))/(RZSM[t-1]*(1-SMrx))))^mr)
    ETs[t]=Es_frac*ETr[t]
    
    # 5. Exclude evaporative losses from SSM
    SSM[t]=ifelse(PCP[t]==0,
                  pmin(por_s,pmax(0.02,(zs*SSM[t]-ETs[t])/zs)),SSM[t])
    
    # Deep drainage based on RZSM state. Continues till CP
    drainage[t]= Ks_r*(pmax(0,RZSM[t-1]-fc_r)/(por_r-fc_r))^b_r
    
    # Update RZSM after drainage and ET
    RZSM[t]=pmin(por_r,pmax(wp_r,
                            ((zr+zs)*RZSM[t-1]+zs*SSM[t]-drainage[t]-ETr[t]+infilt[t])/(zr+zs))) 
  }
  # Return the model output
  return(c(SSM,RZSM,infilt, drainage,ETr,ETs, runoff,PET))
}

############################################################################################
# Model implementation for sample location
############################################################################################

text:
10.1 What we will explore
We will learn how to fit and optimize a physics-based nonlinear response curve in R using NLS2/NLS and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO). We will compare those fitted curves with a Random Forest model that learns the relationship directly from the data. Finally, we will turn the optimization steps into reusable functions and apply them to spatial soil-moisture (SM) and evaporative-fraction (EF) data.
Let’s follow one clear workflow:
observations → physical equation → parameter bounds → optimization → fitted curve → reusable function → parameter maps

The bigger picture



The SM–EF relationship is our case study. The same R workflow can be adapted to other environmental models when you have an equation, unknown parameters, and observations for fitting.

title: 10  Curve Fitting, Optimization, and Machine Learning
text:
10.2 The physical question
Evaporative fraction (EF) describes the fraction of available surface energy used for evapotranspiration. We will model how EF changes as soil moisture (SM) decreases during periods without strong wetting. These periods are called soil-moisture drydowns.
We will represent three soil-moisture regimes:

a dry regime, where water strongly limits EF;
a transition regime, where EF increases with SM; and
a wet regime, where EF reaches a plateau.

10.5 Identify simple drydown periods
Calculate the change in SM from one observation to the next.

eddy_data$SM_change <- c(NA_real_, diff(eddy_data$SM))

A non-increasing step has SM_change <= 0.

eddy_data$is_drydown <-
  is.finite(eddy_data$SM_change) & eddy_data$SM_change <= 0

Create an event number and count the drying steps in each event.

eddy_data$drydown_id <- cumsum(!eddy_data$is_drydown)

eddy_data$drydown_length <- ave(
  eddy_data$is_drydown,
  eddy_data$drydown_id,
  FUN = sum
)

Keep complete SM–EF observations from events with at least five drying steps.

drydown_data <- subset(
  eddy_data,
  is_drydown &
    drydown_length >= min_drydown_steps &
    is.finite(SM) &
    is.finite(EF)
)

title: 10  Curve Fitting, Optimization, and Machine Learning
text:
10.6 Define the physics-based response curve
We will use the following piecewise-linear model:
\[
EF(SM)=
\begin{cases}
0, & SM \leq \theta_d \\
EF_{max}\dfrac{SM-\theta_d}{\theta_w-\theta_d}, & \theta_d < SM < \theta_w \\
EF_{max}, & SM \geq \theta_w.
\end{cases}
\]
The three parameters are:

\(\theta_d\): dry threshold;
\(\theta_w\): wet threshold; and
\(EF_{max}\): EF at the wet plateau.

Translate the equation into an R function.

piecewise_EF <- function(SM, theta_d, theta_w, EF_max) {
  ifelse(
    SM <= theta_d,
    0,
    ifelse(
      SM >= theta_w,
      EF_max,
      EF_max * (SM - theta_d) / (theta_w - theta_d)
    )
  )
}

10.7 Set the optimization bounds
An optimizer searches only inside the parameter space that we allow. We will use the revised bounds below.

lower_bounds <- c(
  theta_d = 0.02,
  theta_w = unname(quantile(drydown_data$SM, 0.35)),
  EF_max = 0.20
)

upper_bounds <- c(
  theta_d = unname(quantile(drydown_data$SM, 0.30)),
  theta_w = unname(quantile(drydown_data$SM, 0.98)),
  EF_max = 1.00
)

lower_bounds

0.0200000 0.1323111 0.2000000 

upper_bounds

  theta_d   theta_w    EF_max 
0.1272590 0.3855175 1.0000000 


Check that every lower bound is smaller than its upper bound.

stopifnot(all(lower_bounds < upper_bounds))







Bounds are part of the model



The dry threshold is searched in the lower part of the observed SM distribution, while the wet threshold is searched in the upper part. This encourages \(\theta_d < \theta_w\) and avoids implausible combinations. If many fitted values reach a bound, inspect the data and reconsider the bound rather than accepting the result automatically.

section: 10.9 Fit the same model with PSO
text:
10.9 Fit the same model with PSO
Particle Swarm Optimization searches with a group of candidate solutions called particles. Each particle moves through the bounded parameter space as the swarm searches for a smaller model error.

10.9.1 Define the objective function
The objective function returns mean squared error. PSO will try to make this value as small as possible.

model_error <- function(parameters, SM, EF) {
  predicted <- piecewise_EF(
    SM,
    theta_d = parameters[1],
    theta_w = parameters[2],
    EF_max = parameters[3]
  )

  mean((EF - predicted)^2, na.rm = TRUE)
}



10.9.2 Run PSO

set.seed(analysis_seed)

pso_fit <- psoptim(
  par = (lower_bounds + upper_bounds) / 2,
  fn = model_error,
  SM = drydown_data$SM,
  EF = drydown_data$EF,
  lower = lower_bounds,
  upper = upper_bounds,
  control = list(
    s = 30,
    maxit = 60,
    trace = 1
  )
)

pso_parameters <- setNames(
  pso_fit$par,
  c("theta_d", "theta_w", "EF_max")
)

pso_parameters

   theta_d    theta_w     EF_max 
0.06190792 0.15777929 0.42608770 








Same equation, different optimization



NLS2/NLS and PSO estimate the same three parameters in the same piecewise model. Differences in their fitted values come from the search algorithms, not from different physical equations.

section: 10.10 Turn the optimizations into reusable functions
text:
10.10 Turn the optimizations into reusable functions
A reusable fitting function should accept two vectors and return one fixed-length parameter vector:
SM + EF \(\rightarrow\) theta_d + theta_w + EF_max

10.10.1 NLS2/NLS function

fit_NLS <- function(SM, EF) {
  keep <- is.finite(SM) & is.finite(EF)
  SM <- SM[keep]
  EF <- EF[keep]

  empty_result <- c(
    theta_d = NA_real_,
    theta_w = NA_real_,
    EF_max = NA_real_
  )

  if (length(SM) < 10 || length(unique(SM)) < 4) {
    return(empty_result)
  }

  lower <- c(
    theta_d = 0.02,
    theta_w = unname(quantile(SM, 0.35)),
    EF_max = 0.20
  )

  upper <- c(
    theta_d = unname(quantile(SM, 0.30)),
    theta_w = unname(quantile(SM, 0.98)),
    EF_max = 1.00
  )

  if (any(!is.finite(c(lower, upper))) || any(lower >= upper)) {
    return(empty_result)
  }

  model_data <- data.frame(SM = SM, EF = EF)

  search_grid <- expand.grid(
    theta_d = seq(lower["theta_d"], upper["theta_d"], length.out = 6),
    theta_w = seq(lower["theta_w"], upper["theta_w"], length.out = 6),
    EF_max = seq(lower["EF_max"], upper["EF_max"], length.out = 6)
  )

  start_fit <- nls2(
    EF ~ piecewise_EF(SM, theta_d, theta_w, EF_max),
    data = model_data,
    start = search_grid,
    algorithm = "brute-force"
  )

  fit <- nls(
    EF ~ piecewise_EF(SM, theta_d, theta_w, EF_max),
    data = model_data,
    start = as.list(coef(start_fit)),
    algorithm = "port",
    lower = lower,
    upper = upper,
    control = nls.control(maxiter = 200, warnOnly = TRUE)
  )

  parameters <- coef(fit)[c("theta_d", "theta_w", "EF_max")]
  setNames(as.numeric(parameters), names(empty_result))
}



10.10.2 PSO function

fit_PSO <- function(SM, EF) {
  keep <- is.finite(SM) & is.finite(EF)
  SM <- SM[keep]
  EF <- EF[keep]

  empty_result <- c(
    theta_d = NA_real_,
    theta_w = NA_real_,
    EF_max = NA_real_
  )

  if (length(SM) < 10 || length(unique(SM)) < 4) {
    return(empty_result)
  }

  lower <- c(
    theta_d = 0.02,
    theta_w = unname(quantile(SM, 0.35)),
    EF_max = 0.20
  )

  upper <- c(
    theta_d = unname(quantile(SM, 0.30)),
    theta_w = unname(quantile(SM, 0.98)),
    EF_max = 1.00
  )

  if (any(!is.finite(c(lower, upper))) || any(lower >= upper)) {
    return(empty_result)
  }

  fit <- psoptim(
    par = (lower + upper) / 2,
    fn = model_error,
    SM = SM,
    EF = EF,
    lower = lower,
    upper = upper,
    control = list(
      s = 30,
      maxit = 60,
      trace = 0
    )
  )

  setNames(as.numeric(fit$par), names(empty_result))
}

text:
10.11 Compare with a Random Forest
A Random Forest learns the SM–EF relationship from many regression trees. It does not assume the three-regime equation and does not directly estimate \(\theta_d\), \(\theta_w\), or \(EF_{max}\). For this reason, it is a useful black-box prediction benchmark, but it is less physically interpretable.

set.seed(analysis_seed)

rf_fit <- randomForest(
  EF ~ SM,
  data = drydown_data,
  ntree = 500,
  mtry = 1,
  nodesize = 10
)

rf_fit


Call:
 randomForest(formula = EF ~ SM, data = drydown_data, ntree = 500,      mtry = 1, nodesize = 10) 
               Type of random forest: regression
                     Number of trees: 500
No. of variables tried at each split: 1

          Mean of squared residuals: 0.01411422
                    % Var explained: 28.71


Create one SM sequence and predict all three fitted responses.

sm_grid <- seq(
  min(drydown_data$SM, na.rm = TRUE),
  max(drydown_data$SM, na.rm = TRUE),
  length.out = 200
)

nls_curve <- piecewise_EF(
  sm_grid,
  nls_parameters["theta_d"],
  nls_parameters["theta_w"],
  nls_parameters["EF_max"]
)

pso_curve <- piecewise_EF(
  sm_grid,
  pso_parameters["theta_d"],
  pso_parameters["theta_w"],
  pso_parameters["EF_max"]
)

rf_curve <- predict(
  rf_fit,
  newdata = data.frame(SM = sm_grid)
)

Plot the methods side by side.

curve_list <- list(
  NLS2 = nls_curve,
  PSO = pso_curve,
  `Random Forest` = rf_curve
)

curve_colors <- c("salmon", "turquoise3", "forestgreen")
old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1))

for (i in seq_along(curve_list)) {
  plot(
    drydown_data$SM,
    drydown_data$EF,
    pch = 16,
    cex = 0.65,
    cex.axis = 1.1,
    cex.lab = 1.1,
    col = adjustcolor("grey30", alpha.f = 0.25),
    panel.first = graphics::grid(),
    xlab = expression("Soil moisture"~(m^3~m^{-3})),
    ylab = if (i == 1) "Evaporative fraction" else "",
    main = names(curve_list)[i]
  )

  lines(
    sm_grid,
    curve_list[[i]],
    col = curve_colors[i],
    lwd = 3
  )
}







par(old_par)







Random Forest is flexible, not physically constrained



The Random Forest response may be step-like or locally non-monotonic. Interpret it only within the SM range represented in the training data. Unlike the piecewise model, it does not provide physically defined threshold parameters.

n_time <- nlyr(SM)
spatial_data <- c(SM, EF)



10.12.4 Add short, safe spatial wrappers
Keep tryCatch() in the full raster calculation so that one failed cell does not stop the complete map.

fit_NLS_spatial <- function(x) {
  SM_cell <- x[1:n_time]
  EF_cell <- x[(n_time + 1):(2 * n_time)]

  tryCatch(
    fit_NLS(SM_cell, EF_cell),
    error = function(e) c(
      theta_d = NA_real_,
      theta_w = NA_real_,
      EF_max = NA_real_
    )
  )
}


fit_PSO_spatial <- function(x) {
  SM_cell <- x[1:n_time]
  EF_cell <- x[(n_time + 1):(2 * n_time)]

  tryCatch(
    fit_PSO(SM_cell, EF_cell),
    error = function(e) c(
      theta_d = NA_real_,
      theta_w = NA_real_,
      EF_max = NA_real_
    )
  )
}







Do not let tryCatch hide the cause



tryCatch() is useful when hundreds of cells are fitted, but it can hide why a model failed. Always test selected cells without tryCatch() before running the complete raster.




10.12.5 Create the parameter maps

nls_parameter_maps <- app(
  spatial_data,
  fit_NLS_spatial
)

names(nls_parameter_maps) <- c("theta_d", "theta_w", "EF_max")







Can we run the spatial optimization in parallel?



Yes. Earlier, we learned that parallel workers run in separate R sessions. When we use multiple cores with terra::app(), objects created in the main R session may not automatically be available to each worker.
We can create a parallel cluster and send the required objects to each worker using clusterExport().
For example, for NLS:

library(parallel)

cl <- makeCluster(4)

clusterExport(
  cl,
  c(
    "n_time",
    "fit_NLS",
    "piecewise_EF"
  )
)

  cl,
  library(nls2)
)

  spatial_data,

For PSO, we would follow the same approach, but export the functions required by the PSO workflow and load the pso package on each worker.
Remember: parallel processing is most useful when the calculation for each cell is computationally expensive. For simple raster operations, the overhead of creating and communicating with workers may actually make the calculation slower. Iterative optimization with NLS or PSO is a much better candidate for parallel processing.

PSO performs an iterative population search in every cell, so its map usually takes longer to compute than the NLS2/NLS map. Run the NLS map first while checking the workflow.

10.13 What should we conclude?

NLS2/NLS and PSO can optimize the same physics-based model with different search strategies.
The optimization bounds directly influence which parameter values can be found.
The piecewise model produces interpretable physical thresholds, while Random Forest provides a flexible black-box comparison.
A function that accepts SM and EF vectors and returns a fixed-length result can be reused for raster-cell calculations.
tryCatch() keeps the full spatial calculation moving, but selected cells should first be tested without it.

In the next chapter, we will ask a new question:

If the fitted parameters change when the data change, how much confidence should we place in one fitted curve or one parameter map?

11.2 Setup and short recap
Install the packages once if needed.

install.packages(c("readr", "minpack.lm", "pso", "randomForest", "terra", "spData"))

Load the packages.

library(readr)
library(minpack.lm)
library(randomForest)

Set the validation choices.

min_drydown_steps <- 5
k_folds <- 5
n_repeats <- 10
analysis_seed <- 100


11.2.1 Read the simplified data

csv_url <- paste0(
  "https://github.com/Vinit-Sehgal/AGRO4092/raw/refs/heads/main/",
  "SampleData-master/US-TON_SM-EF.csv"
)

download.file(
  csv_url,
  destfile = "US-TON_SM-EF.csv",
  mode = "wb"
)


# Read the date column as text before parsing it explicitly.
eddy_data <- read_csv(
  "US-TON_SM-EF.csv",
  col_types = cols(date = col_character()),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# The source file uses month/day/year, such as 5/7/2001.
eddy_data$date <- as.Date(eddy_data$date, format = "%m/%d/%Y")
stopifnot(!anyNA(eddy_data$date))
eddy_data <- eddy_data[order(eddy_data$date), ]



11.2.2 Recreate the drydown data

# Identify consecutive non-increasing SM steps.
eddy_data$SM_change <- c(NA_real_, diff(eddy_data$SM))
eddy_data$is_drydown <-
  is.finite(eddy_data$SM_change) & eddy_data$SM_change <= 0

# Keep each drydown event intact for later resampling.
eddy_data$drydown_id <- cumsum(!eddy_data$is_drydown)
eddy_data$drydown_length <- ave(
  eddy_data$is_drydown,
  eddy_data$drydown_id,
  FUN = sum
)

drydown_data <- subset(
  eddy_data,
  is_drydown &
    drydown_length >= min_drydown_steps &
    is.finite(SM) &
    is.finite(EF)
)

drydown_data$observation_id <- seq_len(nrow(drydown_data))

cat("Observations:", nrow(drydown_data), "\n")

Observations: 4577 

cat("Drydown events:", length(unique(drydown_data$drydown_id)), "\n")

Drydown events: 371 








Keep complete drydowns together



Neighboring observations from one drydown are not independent. We will assign whole drydown events—not individual rows—to training or validation groups. This reduces information leakage.




11.2.3 Reuse the physical model and fitting function
The chapter is self-contained, so we repeat the same physical equation, bounds, and minpack.lm::nlsLM() function used in Chapter 13. Keeping the implementation identical ensures that validation measures changes caused by resampling rather than changes in the model code.

piecewise_EF <- function(SM, theta_d, theta_w, EF_max) {
  # Apply the three physical regimes to every SM value.
  ifelse(
    SM <= theta_d,
    0,
    ifelse(
      SM >= theta_w,
      EF_max,
      EF_max * (SM - theta_d) / (theta_w - theta_d)
    )
  )
}

fit_NLS <- function(SM, EF) {
  # Remove pairs with missing or non-finite values.
  keep <- is.finite(SM) & is.finite(EF)
  SM <- SM[keep]
  EF <- EF[keep]

  # Return this fixed-length vector when a fit is not possible.
  empty_result <- c(
    theta_d = NA_real_,
    theta_w = NA_real_,
    EF_max = NA_real_
  )

  # A nonlinear fit needs enough observations and SM variation.
  if (length(SM) < 10 || length(unique(SM)) < 4) {
    return(empty_result)
  }

  # Recalculate the same bounds for the data supplied to this fit.
  lower <- c(
    theta_d = 0.02,
    theta_w = unname(quantile(SM, 0.35)),
    EF_max = 0.20
  )
  upper <- c(
    theta_d = unname(quantile(SM, 0.30)),
    theta_w = unname(quantile(SM, 0.98)),
    EF_max = 1.00
  )

  if (any(!is.finite(c(lower, upper))) || any(lower >= upper)) {
    return(empty_result)
  }

  # Start at the midpoint of each allowed parameter range.
  start <- (lower + upper) / 2
  model_data <- data.frame(SM = SM, EF = EF)

  fit <- minpack.lm::nlsLM(
    EF ~ piecewise_EF(SM, theta_d, theta_w, EF_max),
    data = model_data,
    start = as.list(start),
    lower = lower,
    upper = upper,
    control = minpack.lm::nls.lm.control(maxiter = 200)
  )

  parameters <- coef(fit)[c("theta_d", "theta_w", "EF_max")]
  setNames(as.numeric(parameters), names(empty_result))
}

Define the validation statistics once so every method is evaluated in the same way.

validation_stats <- function(observed, predicted) {
  # Compare only pairs for which both values are available.
  keep <- complete.cases(observed, predicted)
  observed <- observed[keep]
  predicted <- predicted[keep]

  rmse <- sqrt(mean((observed - predicted)^2))
  mae <- mean(abs(observed - predicted))
  bias <- mean(predicted - observed)

  r2 <- if (length(observed) > 2 &&
            sd(observed) > 0 &&
            sd(predicted) > 0) {
    cor(observed, predicted)^2
  } else {
    NA_real_
  }

  data.frame(RMSE = rmse, MAE = mae, Bias = bias, R2 = r2)
}


RMSE gives more weight to large errors.
MAE is the average absolute error.
Bias is predicted minus observed EF.
\(R^2\) describes association, but it does not measure agreement by itself.

11.3 Begin with one train/test split
A model should be evaluated with observations that were not used to fit it. We first use 80% of the drydown events for training and 20% for testing. This simple split makes the idea of withheld prediction concrete, but its answer depends strongly on which events happen to be selected.

set.seed(analysis_seed)
event_ids <- unique(drydown_data$drydown_id)
train_ids <- sample(event_ids, size = floor(0.80 * length(event_ids)))

# Whole events, rather than individual rows, go to one side of the split.
train_data <- subset(drydown_data, drydown_id %in% train_ids)
test_data <- subset(drydown_data, !drydown_id %in% train_ids)

Fit bounded NLS to the training events and predict the withheld test events. tryCatch() lets the chapter continue with a clear missing result if this one fit fails.

empty_parameters <- c(
  theta_d = NA_real_,
  theta_w = NA_real_,
  EF_max = NA_real_
)

nls_train_parameters <- tryCatch(
  fit_NLS(train_data$SM, train_data$EF),
  error = function(e) empty_parameters
)

nls_test_prediction <- piecewise_EF(
  test_data$SM,
  nls_train_parameters["theta_d"],
  nls_train_parameters["theta_w"],
  nls_train_parameters["EF_max"]
)

Fit Random Forest to the same training events so the comparison uses exactly the same withheld observations.

set.seed(analysis_seed)
rf_train_fit <- randomForest(
  EF ~ SM,
  data = train_data,
  ntree = 500,
  mtry = 1,
  nodesize = 10
)
rf_test_prediction <- predict(rf_train_fit, newdata = test_data)


one_split_results <- rbind(
  NLS = validation_stats(test_data$EF, nls_test_prediction),
  `Random Forest` = validation_stats(test_data$EF, rf_test_prediction)
)
one_split_results

                   RMSE        MAE        Bias        R2
NLS           0.1042303 0.07848923 0.004666457 0.4231526
Random Forest 0.1165519 0.08690832 0.001812429 0.3167515








Why one split is not enough



A favorable split can make a method look better than it usually is, while a difficult split can make it look worse. One split also leaves 20% of the events out of model fitting and evaluates each method on only that one subset. The result describes the chosen split, not the stability of the method across plausible splits.

title: 11  Model Fitting, Optimization, and Uncertainty
text:
11.4 Understand cross-validation before implementing it
Cross-validation is a structured way to repeat the train–test idea. In \(k\)-fold cross-validation, we divide the drydown events into \(k\) groups called folds. We fit the model on \(k-1\) folds, predict the fold that was held out, and rotate the held-out role until every fold has been tested once.
We keep complete drydown events together because neighboring observations within an event are related. Splitting rows from one event across training and testing would let the model see close relatives of the validation observations and could make performance look unrealistically good.






Figure 11.1: Repeated cross-validation. Colors represent observations, and the highlighted column is the fold withheld for testing. The folds are reshuffled for each repeat.



The schematic shows two levels of repetition:

Within one repeat, each of the \(k\) folds is held out once, producing \(k\) fitted models.
Across repeats, the event-to-fold assignment is reshuffled and the full \(k\)-fold cycle is run again.

If we use \(k\) folds and \(n\) repeats, we fit as many as \(k \times n\) models per method. Here, 5 folds and 10 repeats produce up to 50 NLS fits and 50 Random Forest fits. (Some diagrams reverse the letters used for folds and repeats; the important quantity is folds × repeats.)
Repeated \(k \times n\) cross-validation is more informative than one train/test split because:

every event is withheld once in each repeat;
each fit still uses most of the events for training;
reshuffling reveals how sensitive performance and parameters are to the split; and
the many fitted models form an ensemble for summarizing prediction and parameter variation.

Cross-validation does not create independent new data, and its ensemble ranges are not formal confidence intervals. It is a practical diagnostic of out-of-sample performance and resampling sensitivity.

11.5 Implement repeated event-level cross-validation
The code below follows the explanation directly: assign folds, hold one out, fit on the rest, predict the held-out fold, store results, and repeat.

11.5.1 Assign complete events to folds

make_folds <- function(data, k = 5, seed = 100) {
  set.seed(seed)

  # Shuffle event IDs, not individual observations.
  events <- sample(unique(data$drydown_id))
  fold_table <- data.frame(
    drydown_id = events,
    fold = rep(seq_len(k), length.out = length(events))
  )

  # Add the fold number back to every observation in each event.
  merge(data, fold_table, by = "drydown_id", all.x = TRUE, sort = FALSE)
}


example_folds <- make_folds(
  drydown_data,
  k = k_folds,
  seed = analysis_seed
)
table(example_folds$fold)


   1    2    3    4    5 
 786  922  949 1001  919 




11.5.2 Cross-validate the physics-based NLS model

cross_validate_NLS <- function(
    data,
    k = 5,
    repeats = 10,
    seed = 100) {

  parameters <- data.frame()
  statistics <- data.frame()
  predictions <- data.frame()

  for (repeat_id in seq_len(repeats)) {
    # Reshuffle events at the start of each repeat.
    cv_data <- make_folds(data, k = k, seed = seed + repeat_id)

    for (fold_id in seq_len(k)) {
      # Rotate one fold into validation; fit on all remaining folds.
      train <- subset(cv_data, fold != fold_id)
      test <- subset(cv_data, fold == fold_id)

      pars <- tryCatch(
        fit_NLS(train$SM, train$EF),
        error = function(e) c(
          theta_d = NA_real_,
          theta_w = NA_real_,
          EF_max = NA_real_
        )
      )

      # Skip a failed fit but continue the other folds.
      if (length(pars) != 3 || any(!is.finite(pars))) {
        next
      }

      # Predict only observations withheld from this fit.
      predicted <- piecewise_EF(
        test$SM,
        pars["theta_d"],
        pars["theta_w"],
        pars["EF_max"]
      )

      parameters <- rbind(
        parameters,
        data.frame(
          repeat_id = repeat_id,
          fold_id = fold_id,
          method = "NLS",
          theta_d = unname(pars["theta_d"]),
          theta_w = unname(pars["theta_w"]),
          EF_max = unname(pars["EF_max"])
        )
      )

      fold_stats <- validation_stats(test$EF, predicted)
      fold_stats$repeat_id <- repeat_id
      fold_stats$fold_id <- fold_id
      fold_stats$method <- "NLS"
      statistics <- rbind(statistics, fold_stats)

      predictions <- rbind(
        predictions,
        data.frame(
          repeat_id = repeat_id,
          fold_id = fold_id,
          method = "NLS",
          observation_id = test$observation_id,
          SM = test$SM,
          EF_observed = test$EF,
          EF_predicted = predicted
        )
      )
    }
  }

  list(
    parameters = parameters,
    statistics = statistics,
    predictions = predictions
  )
}

Run the repeated 5-fold workflow.

nls_results <- cross_validate_NLS(
  drydown_data,
  k = k_folds,
  repeats = n_repeats,
  seed = analysis_seed
)

nls_parameters <- nls_results$parameters
nls_statistics <- nls_results$statistics
nls_predictions <- nls_results$predictions







Use tryCatch only after testing one fold



tryCatch() keeps a long resampling run moving when one fit fails, but it can hide the original error. While developing the workflow, run one selected training fold directly with fit_NLS() and inspect any failure before using the wrapper.








Optional replacement: cross-validate with PSO



Cross-validation does not depend on the optimizer. After defining fit_PSO() as shown in Chapter 13, replace this line inside the fold loop:

pars <- fit_NLS(train$SM, train$EF)

with:

set.seed(seed + 1000 * repeat_id + fold_id)
pars <- fit_PSO(train$SM, train$EF)

Keep the folds, withheld predictions, statistics, and output structure unchanged. PSO then becomes an alternative optimizer for the same physical equation rather than a separate validation workflow.




11.5.3 Cross-validate Random Forest on the same folds

rf_statistics <- data.frame()
rf_predictions <- data.frame()
rf_models <- list()

for (repeat_id in seq_len(n_repeats)) {
  # Reuse the same seeds so both methods receive the same folds.
  cv_data <- make_folds(
    drydown_data,
    k = k_folds,
    seed = analysis_seed + repeat_id
  )

  for (fold_id in seq_len(k_folds)) {
    train <- subset(cv_data, fold != fold_id)
    test <- subset(cv_data, fold == fold_id)

    fit <- tryCatch(
      {
        set.seed(analysis_seed + 1000 * repeat_id + fold_id)
        randomForest(
          EF ~ SM,
          data = train,
          ntree = 500,
          mtry = 1,
          nodesize = 10
        )
      },
      error = function(e) NULL
    )

    if (is.null(fit)) next

    predicted <- predict(fit, newdata = test)
    fold_stats <- validation_stats(test$EF, predicted)
    fold_stats$repeat_id <- repeat_id
    fold_stats$fold_id <- fold_id
    fold_stats$method <- "Random Forest"
    rf_statistics <- rbind(rf_statistics, fold_stats)

    rf_predictions <- rbind(
      rf_predictions,
      data.frame(
        repeat_id = repeat_id,
        fold_id = fold_id,
        method = "Random Forest",
        observation_id = test$observation_id,
        SM = test$SM,
        EF_observed = test$EF,
        EF_predicted = as.numeric(predicted)
      )
    )

    rf_models[[length(rf_models) + 1]] <- fit
  }
}

11.7 Examine NLS parameter uncertainty
The 50 repeat-fold fits can return 50 estimates of each physical parameter. Their spread shows how sensitive the fitted thresholds are to the training drydowns.

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1))

boxplot(nls_parameters$EF_max, col = "salmon", ylab = expression(EF[max]), main = "Wet plateau")







par(old_par)


parameter_range <- function(x) {
  c(
    median = median(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    lower = quantile(x, 0.025, na.rm = TRUE, names = FALSE),
    upper = quantile(x, 0.975, na.rm = TRUE, names = FALSE)
  )
}

sapply(
  nls_parameters[c("theta_d", "theta_w", "EF_max")],
  parameter_range

A narrow ensemble is not automatically trustworthy. If many estimates collect at a lower or upper bound, the data may not constrain that parameter, or the search space may need reconsideration.

text:
11.8 Examine prediction uncertainty
Predict EF over one SM grid with every repeat-fold model. At each SM value, summarize the median and the 2.5th–97.5th percentile ensemble range.

sm_grid <- seq(
  min(drydown_data$SM, na.rm = TRUE),
  max(drydown_data$SM, na.rm = TRUE),
  length.out = 200
)

# Columns are ensemble members; rows are SM values.
nls_curve_matrix <- matrix(
  NA_real_,
  nrow = length(sm_grid),
  ncol = nrow(nls_parameters)
)
for (i in seq_len(nrow(nls_parameters))) {
  nls_curve_matrix[, i] <- piecewise_EF(
    sm_grid,
    nls_parameters$theta_d[i],
    nls_parameters$theta_w[i],
    nls_parameters$EF_max[i]
  )
}

rf_curve_matrix <- matrix(
  NA_real_,
  nrow = length(sm_grid),
  ncol = length(rf_models)
)
for (i in seq_along(rf_models)) {
  rf_curve_matrix[, i] <- predict(
    rf_models[[i]],
    newdata = data.frame(SM = sm_grid)
  )
}


summarize_curves <- function(prediction_matrix) {
  data.frame(
    SM = sm_grid,
    EF_median = apply(prediction_matrix, 1, median, na.rm = TRUE),
    EF_lower = apply(prediction_matrix, 1, quantile, probs = 0.025, na.rm = TRUE),
    EF_upper = apply(prediction_matrix, 1, quantile, probs = 0.975, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
}

nls_curve_summary <- summarize_curves(nls_curve_matrix)
rf_curve_summary <- summarize_curves(rf_curve_matrix)


curve_list <- list(NLS = nls_curve_summary, `Random Forest` = rf_curve_summary)
curve_colors <- c("salmon", "forestgreen")
old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1))

for (i in seq_along(curve_list)) {
  s <- curve_list[[i]]
  plot(
    drydown_data$SM,
    drydown_data$EF,
    pch = 16,
    cex = 0.65,
    col = adjustcolor("grey30", alpha.f = 0.25),
    panel.first = graphics::grid(),
    xlab = expression("Soil moisture"~(m^3~m^{-3})),
    ylab = if (i == 1) "Evaporative fraction" else "",
    main = names(curve_list)[i]
  )
  polygon(
    c(s$SM, rev(s$SM)),
    c(s$EF_lower, rev(s$EF_upper)),
    col = adjustcolor(curve_colors[i], alpha.f = 0.20),
    border = NA
  )
  lines(s$SM, s$EF_median, col = curve_colors[i], lwd = 3)
}







par(old_par)







The ribbon is an ensemble range



The ribbon describes variation among repeat-fold model fits. It is not a formal confidence interval and does not include every source of measurement, parameter, and model-structure uncertainty.

11.10 Map spatial parameter uncertainty
Chapter 13 produced one NLS parameter value per raster cell. Here we repeatedly fit 80% subsamples within each cell and summarize how much the fitted NLS parameters change. This spatial resampling estimates parameter sensitivity; it is not the event-level cross-validation used above to estimate predictive performance.

11.10.1 Read the matched raster time series

library(terra)
library(spData)


# Download and read the matched time series.
download.file(
  "https://github.com/Vinit-Sehgal/AGRO4092/raw/refs/heads/main/SampleData-master/SM.nc",
  destfile = "SM.nc",
  mode = "wb"
)
download.file(
  "https://github.com/Vinit-Sehgal/AGRO4092/raw/refs/heads/main/SampleData-master/EF.nc",
  destfile = "EF.nc",
  mode = "wb"
)
SM <- rast("SM.nc")
EF <- rast("EF.nc")

stopifnot(compareGeom(SM, EF, stopOnError = FALSE))
stopifnot(nlyr(SM) == nlyr(EF))



11.10.2 Test resampling for one cell

# Select a well-observed cell.
complete_count <- xapp(
  SM,
  EF,
  fun = function(SM, EF) sum(is.finite(SM) & is.finite(EF))
)
cell_id <- which.max(values(complete_count, mat = FALSE))
cell_SM <- as.numeric(extract(SM, cell_id, raw = TRUE))
cell_EF <- as.numeric(extract(EF, cell_id, raw = TRUE))

n_spatial_samples <- 20
sample_fraction <- 0.80
keep <- is.finite(cell_SM) & is.finite(cell_EF)
cell_SM <- cell_SM[keep]
cell_EF <- cell_EF[keep]

cell_parameters <- matrix(
  NA_real_,
  nrow = n_spatial_samples,
  ncol = 3,
  dimnames = list(NULL, c("theta_d", "theta_w", "EF_max"))
)

set.seed(analysis_seed)
for (i in seq_len(n_spatial_samples)) {
  # Draw a different 80% subset without replacement.
  sample_id <- sample(
    seq_along(cell_SM),
    size = floor(sample_fraction * length(cell_SM)),
    replace = FALSE
  )

  cell_parameters[i, ] <- tryCatch(
    fit_NLS(cell_SM[sample_id], cell_EF[sample_id]),
    error = function(e) c(
      theta_d = NA_real_,
      theta_w = NA_real_,
      EF_max = NA_real_
    )
  )
}

apply(cell_parameters, 2, parameter_range)

11.10.3 Write the cell-wise uncertainty function

spatial_summary <- function(x) {
  lower <- quantile(x, 0.025, na.rm = TRUE, names = FALSE)
  upper <- quantile(x, 0.975, na.rm = TRUE, names = FALSE)
  c(
    median = median(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    lower = lower,
    upper = upper,
    width = upper - lower
  )
}

n_time <- nlyr(SM)
spatial_data <- c(SM, EF)

fit_NLS_uncertainty <- function(x) {
  # Separate the combined cell vector into SM and EF.
  SM_cell <- x[seq_len(n_time)]
  EF_cell <- x[n_time + seq_len(n_time)]
  keep <- is.finite(SM_cell) & is.finite(EF_cell)
  SM_cell <- SM_cell[keep]
  EF_cell <- EF_cell[keep]

  empty_result <- rep(NA_real_, 12)
  if (length(SM_cell) < 20 || length(unique(SM_cell)) < 4) {
    return(empty_result)
  }

  fitted_parameters <- matrix(
    NA_real_,
    nrow = n_spatial_samples,
    ncol = 3
  )

  # Use a reproducible sequence of subsamples within each cell.
  set.seed(analysis_seed)
  for (i in seq_len(n_spatial_samples)) {
    sample_id <- sample(
      seq_along(SM_cell),
      size = floor(sample_fraction * length(SM_cell)),
      replace = FALSE
    )

    fitted_parameters[i, ] <- tryCatch(
      fit_NLS(SM_cell[sample_id], EF_cell[sample_id]),
      error = function(e) c(
        theta_d = NA_real_,
        theta_w = NA_real_,
        EF_max = NA_real_
      )
    )
  }

  fitted_parameters <- fitted_parameters[
    complete.cases(fitted_parameters),
    ,
    drop = FALSE
  ]
  if (nrow(fitted_parameters) < 5) return(empty_result)

  c(
    spatial_summary(fitted_parameters[, 1]),
    spatial_summary(fitted_parameters[, 2]),
    spatial_summary(fitted_parameters[, 3])
  )
}







Optional spatial replacement with PSO



To use PSO for the same spatial resampling, define fit_PSO() as in Chapter 13 and replace:

fit_NLS(SM_cell[sample_id], EF_cell[sample_id])

with:

fit_PSO(SM_cell[sample_id], EF_cell[sample_id])

Keep the subsampling, summaries, layer names, and tryCatch() structure unchanged.




11.10.4 Create spatial uncertainty layers

spatial_uncertainty <- terra::app(
  spatial_data,
  fit_NLS_uncertainty
)

names(spatial_uncertainty) <- c(
  "theta_d_median", "theta_d_lower", "theta_d_upper", "theta_d_width",
  "theta_w_median", "theta_w_lower", "theta_w_upper", "theta_w_width",
  "EF_max_median", "EF_max_lower", "EF_max_upper", "EF_max_width"
)

Twenty resamples keep the teaching example manageable. A research analysis may use more after the function has been tested carefully.


11.10.5 Plot median parameters and uncertainty widths
Use terra::plot() for the maps and legends. The fun argument adds state boundaries after each layer without manual legend code.

states <- project(vect(spData::us_states), crs(SM))
add_states <- function() {
  terra::lines(states, col = "grey20", lwd = 0.8)
}


median_maps <- spatial_uncertainty[[c(
  "theta_d_median",
  "theta_w_median",
  "EF_max_median"
)]]

terra::plot(
  median_maps,
  main = c(
    expression("Median"~theta[d]),
    expression("Median"~theta[w]),
    expression("Median"~EF[max])
  ),
  fun = add_states,
  nc = 1
)









width_maps <- spatial_uncertainty[[c(
  "theta_d_width",
  "theta_w_width",
  "EF_max_width"
)]]

terra::plot(
  width_maps,
  main = c(
    expression("95% ensemble width for"~theta[d]),
    expression("95% ensemble width for"~theta[w]),
    expression("95% ensemble width for"~EF[max])
  ),
  fun = add_states,
  nc = 1
)








Large width values identify cells where fitted parameters are especially sensitive to the selected observations.

11.11 What should we conclude?

One train/test split introduces withheld prediction but is sensitive to one random partition.
Repeated \(k \times n\) cross-validation rotates the test fold and reshuffles assignments, producing a more stable view of out-of-sample performance.
Keeping complete drydown events together reduces information leakage.
minpack.lm::nlsLM() remains the consistent physics-based model, while Random Forest is the black-box comparison.
Repeat-fold NLS fits create distributions of parameters and predictions; their ranges are diagnostics, not formal confidence intervals.
Spatial resampling maps where NLS parameters are stable and where they are sensitive to the selected observations.
PSO can replace the optimizer without changing the folds, physical equation, summaries, or spatial workflow.
